chapter: Young players, schools and studio work
title: School stage bands and ruined lips
summary: Hinton on stage band adjudication; Maxwell says directors ruin students' lips with Maynard Ferguson charts.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: Now, you were saying -- I'm inclined to agree with you, there's no substitute for the experience of being in a road band. And we're so lacking in the number of bands that young people can get their experience in. There are very few bands around where that can happen.

I was wondering, what is your experience and your idea about a stage band? I see all over the country stage / stage bands and these semester of learning young people have a whole/ one or two arrangements and then come experience to adjudicate these bands-- up playing absolutely beautiful. It's been my / these young people, and they were coming to make their presentation and present what they'd been working on. And then we convene in another room and we have a given chart, pretty simple, for them to read, sight in this room read. And they'll stay /and they were given five minutes to look

at this piece of music. They couldn't play their instruments at all, just look at it. And the leader, the conductor, hum the part, tell them, watch out for this. And then we as judges would judge them on how they read it, how they interpreted dynamics, and so forth. And we found that there was a whale of difference between what they had worked on all the semester and what they know about the reading of -- or getting up and improvising a solo. How do you feel about that?

Well, I feel very strongly, from a trumpet player's point of view, because I have met several of these young people who are real hotshots in the college and high school bands. And many of these conductors, in the departments, they want to get a big reputation and they don't care what they do to their kids' lips. And they'll have one kid there, he can jam the mouthpiece and twist it in his lip and hit a high G that will shake the room. And he can't do anything else and he'll sit there and wait for these high parts.

And they get these Maynard Ferguson arrangements for the stage bands, and the arrangement that the average professional musician would refuse to play, you know, they're very specialized kinds of things. And they batter their lips and they spend the whole term learning these things. They come out of school with a very inflated ego and they run into some very traumatic experience. I have two or three people out of college bands, exactly like that, who've come to me. They said,

you know, Mr. Maxwell, I really don't know how to play the trumpet. I can play good high G's, you know, but I want to learn how to play the melody, I want to know how to get a decent sound. And they don't know those things. They can't read. And it's sort of sad.

I don't say that all schools are like that because naturally, I don't get the successful ones who came from schools where that didn't happen. But there are some schools where the teacher, I'm sure his only motive is to get a big reputation for his band, and he doesn't care what he's done.
I agree with you and I'm disturbed about that, about our young people. I'm sure that all bands aren't like that, all schools aren't like that.
I've found the same thing, too, Jimmy, in my experience. You want to elaborate on that any more? I have a couple more questions to ask you.
Yeah, surely. No, I think I've said about all I have to say on that, as far as the teaching angle.
